new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (30 pp., no text layer) and rendered pdf pp. 2, 7, 9 at 110 dpi to check the page images directly, not just the scanned file. Page images carry the running heads '14 Robbins Burling and L. Amon Phom', 'Phom Phonology and Word List 19' and '.. 21', so the stated offset (pdf N = printed 12+N) holds. All three quoted sentences are on the page images exactly as quoted: p. 14 last paragraph 'Phom does turn out to be a tone language, and like many such languages of East and Southeast Asia, its sound system is most easily described in terms of its syllables and their parts: 1. Initial consonants, 2. Vowels, 3. Final consonants, 4. Tones.'; p. 19 under '5.0. TONES': 'Three distinct tones can…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Phom is described as a lexical tone language: every syllable carries one of three tones (/55/ high level, /33/ mid level, /31/ mid-to-low falling; glottal-final syllables toneless), polysyllables are simply concatenations of fully toned syllables with no reduced or 'minor' syllables and no tone-sequence restrictions. No source examined describes word stress, accent, or prominence at all; none says stress is absent either. Bano 2008 (p. 168) adds a tone-placement generalization ('the high tones are usually marked on the second syllable' of bi-/tri-syllabic words, on the first if the second is glottal-stopped) and Phom 2018 (p. 112) finds tone alternation 'biased to the left sided syllables' in derived disyllables, but both concern tone, not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal: syllables ending in /ʔ/ show no tonal contrast (Burling & Phom p. 19); tone /31/ is rare on stopped syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (monosyllables and compounds/derived polysyllables in citation form). Phom 2018 recorded words in isolation and in a carrier sentence and found tones stable across contexts (no tone sandhi). Burling & Phom's data come from co-author L. Amon Phom, a native speaker from the lower Tamlu area; Phom 2018 (pp. 12-16) notes dialect differences (Yongyah standard vs. lower Tamlu villages, e.g. absence of /ɣ/ there).
new_statements.identity_note: All three opened sources describe the Phom of Longleng district, Nagaland (phom1236). Burling & Phom 1998 reflects one speaker (L. Amon Phom) from the lower Tamlu villages; Phom 2018 uses speakers of the Yongyah (standard) dialect and lists dialect differences in ch. 1 (pp. 12-16) and Appendix III. No separate glottocodes exist for these dialects.

sources.locator: p. 14 (§1.0 Introduction), p. 19 (§5.0 Tones), p. 21 (§6.0 Polysyllables); pdf pp. 2, 7, 9
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent. Phom is 'a tone language' (p. 14); section 5.0 TONES (p. 19) gives three tones /55/ high level, /33/ mid level, /31/ falling; syllables in /-ʔ/ show no tonal contrast; 'no restrictions on tone sequences', tones of polysyllables identified with those of monosyllables, and no reduced 'half'/'minor' syllables (p. 21). The word 'stress' does not occur in the scanned text (only 'strongly accented' in a comparison with an English vowel, p. 16).

sources.note: No stress finding. Lists 'the effect of the stress plays on the tone in the language' among its objectives (p. 104) but reports none; one offhand remark that consonant clusters in derived polysyllables 'are pronounced with the same amount of stress as different syllables' (p. 29-30). Acoustically confirms three tones (high and mid level, low falling; p. 111); in disyllables both syllables keep their lexical tones, but tone alternation is 'biased' to one syllable: 'In derived disyllables, the tone change is biased to the left sided syllables, while the right sided syllables or suffixes usually…
